🤖 # Research

The immutable v0 pool in [#10314](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10314) contains 100,000 selected contracts, including Eurus2 and historical native imports. The Eurus2 converter copies every source `prompt` message into the model-visible TaskSpec, and its review rubric explicitly says to preserve every message; neither step removes instructions such as `[ASSESS]` or `Next action:`. The grader is built from hidden `reward_model.ground_truth` tests, so prompt editing needs a separate verifier check. No open PR matched #10350 or Eurus2; [#10319](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10319) covers native import/runtime work.

**Relevant code**
- [`skyrl/code.py#L56-L60`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d2fd52791f480c0510bf354c5f785013ffef001/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/code.py#L56-L60) — Eurus2 preservation rubric
- [`skyrl/code.py#L198-L206`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d2fd52791f480c0510bf354c5f785013ffef001/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/code.py#L198-L206) — source messages copied into TaskSpec
- [`skyrl/code.py#L169-L191`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d2fd52791f480c0510bf354c5f785013ffef001/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/code.py#L169-L191) — hidden tests and required answer format
- [`models.py#L851-L868`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d2fd52791f480c0510bf354c5f785013ffef001/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/models.py#L851-L868) — TaskSpec prompt and grader boundary

# Proposed Fix

1. Pin the `2026.10.19.2` manifest and scan all 100,000 selected records, parsing canonical `task_json` and native `lowered_task_spec` by `contract_kind`. Inspect every model-visible instruction/message, seeding detection with the linked Eurus2 action labels, numbered reasoning steps, and `Next action:`; review equivalent directives across sources. Manually adjudicate every candidate and a source-stratified sample of unflagged tasks. Publish affected task IDs and counts by source and family, with explicit `prune`, `keep-required-format`, and `quarantine` decisions. Preserve source aliases and the full 100,000-row denominator.
2. Build deterministic, reviewed edits that delete only instructions prescribing a reasoning style. Retain each problem, context, tool/action interface, verifier-required output syntax, and private grading contract. Record original and cleaned payload hashes, edited spans, decision reason, source locator, and reviewer decision for each affected ID; leave ambiguous records quarantined. Update the Eurus2 converter/rubric so later curation runs apply the same rule, with fixtures covering the linked task, required Python output format, and legitimate task-specific procedures.
3. Publish a new immutable pool version derived from `2026.10.19.2`, with its parent manifest hash, transformation code revision, all row mappings, per-source counts, quarantine list, and public before/after examples including `eurus2_code-004832f8a66c2fafab97e3d76bfbbc0d6885291f3578e356ec3d95c610e6ad4b`. Recheck task IDs, full-contract deduplication, known holdouts, family quotas, and trainer loading. If quarantine or newly merged contracts reduce the pool, refill only from the pinned eligible candidate set under the existing selection policy and record replacements; otherwise report the shortfall.
4. Run the same pinned grader on representative original and cleaned tasks from every affected source, using known-valid and known-invalid completions and requiring unchanged verdicts. Eurus2 has no published golden completion in the converter, so obtain an independently verified positive example before treating its grader comparison as passed. Hold any task with a changed verdict or unresolved ambiguity out of the training-ready release.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Three matched mixed-domain RLVR runs from the Grug Datakit SFT (October 5) test whether a share of [PivotRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) pivots improves SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite without hurting the other domains, and whether pivot selection matters: RLVR alone, RLVR with selected SWE and Terminal pivots at 20% of prompts, and RLVR with random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share. Two optional arms move the selected share to 10% and 30%. Every arm stops at 12 steps. Status: all three arms trained 12 steps at seed 42 and were evaluated at steps 4, 8 and 12; [results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214#issuecomment-6305992938). B is the only arm above the SFT on SWE-bench Verified (+8.8 points at steps 4 and 8, p=.0001; +4.8 at step 12), C never transfers, and every arm drifts on Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12, B least. A seed-43 replicate is training.

## Hypothesis

Pivots that the SFT policy's own pass rates select (#9933), rewarded by #9933's deterministic verifiers, improve SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite at 20% of prompts while broad holdout accuracy stays within noise. Random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share help less. Training pivots alone has been hard to stabilize; mixing them into broad RLVR keeps the rest of the policy anchored.

## Setup

- **Start:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05), a pure SFT checkpoint. #9933 measured its SWE and Terminal pass rates on this policy, so the selections apply unchanged, and the RLVR data is unseen.
- **RLVR data:** [Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30) (84,403 train / 94 validation rows; 24% single-step tool use, 14% instruction following, 9% code, 13% math, no SWE or Terminal rows). Any SWE or terminal change between arms is therefore attributable to the added turns.
- **Recipe:** the #9735 reference/KL arm (frozen reference, KL 0.01, sequence-mean loss, entropy 0.001, router replay), 512 prompts × 16 samples per step, at most 12 steps, the same seed in every arm. SFT starts in #9735 collapsed after 12 to 20 steps. Asynchronous rollouts with staleness up to 2, TIS correction, a 102,400-token request window with 49,152 tokens per turn, and thinking on, as #9933 measured the pivots' pass rates.
- **RLVR blend as trained:** 63,590 of RLVR1's rows. MarinSkyRL now runs every Nemotron Ultra row as a task session, and code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, so every arm omits those four agents (about 20% of RLVR1, including #9735's code domain). Rows containing a blank text message, which task conversations reject, are dropped too (3,991 RLVR, 59 Terminal). Validation keeps 67 of RLVR1's 94 rows.
- **Pivot prompts:** the runtime drops earlier assistant turns' reasoning from pivot prompts, which #9933's pass-rate measurement kept.
- **Pivots:** #9933's long-format SWE and Terminal candidates, selected at λ = 0.65 (1 to 10 passes of 16) from the pooled K = 16 pass rates already measured on this policy (`users/dml/pivotrl/{swe,terminal}/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005+seed-1@2026.10.09`). That selects 25,792 of 72,434 scored SWE turns under `nemo` and 6,999 of 36,107 Terminal turns.
- **Reward:** `nemotron_ultra` grades pivot rows through MarinSkyRL#992 with #9933's verifiers: NeMo Gym argument comparison (`nemo`) for SWE and Terminus-2 keystroke similarity without a judge (`string_90`) for Terminal. #10000 uses the same graders. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap the pass rates were sampled at.

## Arms

| Arm | Data |
| --- | --- |
| A | RLVR1 |
| B | RLVR1, with selected pivots replacing 20% of prompts |
| C | RLVR1, with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns replacing 20% of prompts |
| B-10, B-30 (optional) | As B, at 10% and 30% |

The batch stays at 512 prompts, so added turns displace RLVR prompts. Each step carries 102 added turns, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal, because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling fills every batch to these counts from route-tagged pools and draws each pool uniformly. RLVR rows come first and their pool is shuffled first, so with one seed B's and C's RLVR prompts are a prefix of A's draw order. Twelve steps use 612 of each pool (25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots), so no turn repeats.

### Why 20%

Only groups with mixed outcomes produce a gradient, and RLVR1 groups already mostly do: `reward/informative_group_fraction` was 0.79 at the first step from the Datakit SFT (Datakit v4, #9735) and fell to about 0.55 by step 12. Resampling the stored K = 16 pass rates, 88% of selected SWE pivots and 81% of selected Terminal pivots come back mixed, against 58% and 24% of random candidate turns. Pivots' share of the gradient is therefore only 1.1 to 1.5 times their share of prompts, and C carries about half of B's pivot signal at the same share.

Pivot-only RL on this SFT, with the same policy learning rate (4e-6) and gradient clip, bounds the dose. One update of 64 SWE pivot groups raised SWE-bench Verified from 26.0% to 29.4% (146 vs 129 of 496 matched tasks, against a historical base run) with AIME24 unchanged; five updates raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.29 to 0.38. Forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24 and 9 to 10 on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, and ninety SWE updates collapsed agentic behavior (1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved, 0 of 190 TBLite) while held-out pivot accuracy kept rising.

Counting a mixed step as its pivot gradient share of a pivot-only update, with RLVR1's informative fraction averaging about 0.68 over the first 12 steps, a first-order approximation that ignores RLVR and KL counteracting drift:

| *p* | Pivot prompts per step | Pivot gradient share | Equivalent pivot-only updates by step 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10% | 51 | ~12% | ~1.5 |
| 20% | 102 | ~24% | ~2.9 |
| 30% | 154 | ~35% | ~4.2 |

With at most 12 steps, 10% delivers about one pivot-only update, the dose that gained about 3 points on SWE, below what the benchmarks resolve. 20% places the dose in the middle of the range where pivot-only training helped, about 14 times below where it did damage, with RLVR still about three quarters of the gradient. B-10 and B-30 bracket it.

## Measurements

- At steps 0, 4, 8 and 12: pass rate on #9933's held-out validation turns graded in process, broad holdout pass@1 and normalized verifier score, and per-domain reward.
- Per step and per source (RLVR, SWE, Terminal): informative group count and mean response length, so B and C are compared by delivered pivot signal and any pull toward shorter RLVR answers shows up early. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap their pass rates were sampled at, through each pivot row's request; the sequence-mean loss weights them like full RLVR answers.
- At step 0 and each arm's step 4, 8 and 12 checkpoints: full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (Terminus 2), three runs each, compared per task between arms, plus AIME24, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, the benchmarks pivot-only training hurt.
- Checkpoints are selected by the broad holdout and pivot validation, never by the benchmarks. A paired comparison on 500 SWE tasks has a standard error of about 2 points; on 100 tasks it is about 4.4, too wide for the effects expected here.

## Decision rules

- B beats A on SWE-bench Verified or OpenThoughts-TBLite by more than two paired standard errors, with the broad holdout and the four reasoning benchmarks within noise: pivots help in mixed RLVR. Next, test RL-then-merge against the Campaign 3 merge recipe (#9975).
- B ≈ C: selection does not matter at this share; random turns are enough. B > C partly reflects C's smaller pivot signal, so the logged informative group counts qualify the comparison.
- B beats A on pivot validation only: the verifier reward does not transfer to the benchmarks. Revisit the reward component (`exact`) or the generation cap.
- An arm collapses: report its best checkpoint before the collapse and compare arms only at matched steps.

## Prerequisites

1. Per-agent `pivot_reward`, declared among the Nemotron Ultra session settings: MarinSkyRL#992.
2. Selection artifacts at λ = 0.65 from #9933's stored K = 16 pass rates: built, 25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots.
3. 4. A two-step smoke run of B on 6 nodes (64 prompts with B's composition, 32K window) confirming that every agent's rows load and grade.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Results for the three arms at steps 4, 8 and 12, paired per item against the October 5 Datakit SFT (REF). One run per arm at seed 42. Training runs: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/1u013rdm), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/e01zoz2k), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/zblphp52). A12's SWE-bench job is still retrying verifier timeouts, so that one cell is provisional; the rest of the 54 evaluations are final.

Selected pivots are the only treatment that moves SWE-bench Verified, the effect is present at step 4, and random turns at the same share do not transfer. Every arm erodes Math500 and MMLU-Pro by step 12; B erodes least. Step 8 is the checkpoint to report.

## SWE-bench Verified

Strict scoring: a trial with no verifier result counts as unsolved, each cell is one complete 500-task run, and p-values are exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs.

| Step | REF | A | B | C | B vs A | B vs C | B vs REF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | .260 | .288 | .348 | .232 | +6.0, p=.004 | +11.6, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 8 | .260 | .256 | .348 | .248 | +9.2, p<.0001 | +10.0, p<.0001 | +8.8, p=.0001 |
| 12 | .260 | .272 (provisional) | .308 | .244 | +3.6, p=.07 | +6.4, p=.002 | +4.8, p=.025 |

A and C never differ from REF (every |Δ| ≤ 2.8 points, p ≥ .14). B newly solves 22 to 23% of the tasks REF fails, against 10 to 15% for A and C, and keeps about 70% of REF's solved tasks. B12 vs B8 is −4.0 (p=.054).

## Other benchmarks

Δ vs REF in points. GPQA-Diamond averages 3 trials per question and AIME24 10, tested with a paired sign-flip permutation test; Math500 and MMLU-Pro use exact McNemar; OT-TBLite counts a task solved when at least 2 of 3 trials score 1. Starred cells have p<.05.

| Step | Arm | GPQA-D | MMLU-Pro | Math500 | AIME24 | OT-TBLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | A | +3.9 | +0.9 ★ | 0.0 | −3.3 | +2.0 |
| 4 | B | +6.4 ★ | +0.6 | −0.8 | −0.7 | +3.0 |
| 4 | C | +7.6 ★ | 0.0 | −0.8 | −1.7 | 0.0 |
| 8 | A | +6.2 ★ | +0.8 ★ | −0.2 | +1.0 | −5.0 |
| 8 | B | +7.4 ★ | +0.4 | 0.0 | −3.0 | −2.0 |
| 8 | C | +6.1 ★ | +0.4 | −1.0 | 0.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | A | +5.7 ★ | −1.6 ★ | −7.6 ★ | −4.0 | −4.0 |
| 12 | B | +6.6 ★ | −1.1 ★ | −2.2 (p=.052) | 0.0 | −3.0 |
| 12 | C | +4.5 ★ | −3.4 ★ | −7.8 ★ | −0.3 | −3.0 |

REF accuracies: GPQA-Diamond .635 (n=198), MMLU-Pro .780 (n=12032), Math500 .968 (n=500), AIME24 .830 (n=30), OT-TBLite .16 (n=100). At step 12 B beats A by +5.4 and C by +5.6 on Math500 (both p<.0001) and C by +2.3 on MMLU-Pro (p<.0001). No arm differs from another on GPQA-Diamond or AIME24 at any step, and TBLite with 100 tasks cannot resolve differences under about 9 points.

## Reading

Random turns are the control that makes the SWE-bench result interpretable. C uses the same turn sources, verifiers and share as B, and on the held-out pivot turns it learns the pivot task as fast as B: SWE pivot pass@1 rises from .24 to .42 in both arms and Terminal from .15 to .23, while A stays at .23. Only the selected turns transfer to the benchmark. Random turns also carry less signal, as the plan anticipated: informative-group fraction 0.59 against 0.67 for A and B, and pivot rewards about half of B's.

The GPQA gain of 4 to 8 points in every arm from step 4 comes from the RLVR mix.

The step-12 losses are on hard multi-step items. On Math500, levels 1 to 3 move within 3 points in every arm; level 4 drops 7.8 (A), 2.3 (B) and 8.6 (C) points and level 5 drops 17.2, 4.5 and 15.7. On MMLU-Pro, which is decoded greedily, the losses sit in engineering, chemistry, physics and math; B12 is flat on engineering where A12 is −5.8 and C12 −7.7. The lost Math500 answers run 4.3 times the length of REF's answer to the same question and 34 of A12's 42 end in an extracted wrong answer rather than a truncation. The share of Math500 responses over 100K characters is 0.4% for REF, 4.8% for A4, 8.2% for B12, 11.0% for C12 and 12.4% for A12.

The training curves carry the same signature. Policy entropy rises every step (A 0.83 to 2.76, B to 1.95, C to 2.18) and KL to the frozen reference climbs with no plateau (A .071, B .063, C .086 at step 12), so the 0.01 KL coefficient does not hold the policy. The arm that drifts least degrades least. The in-distribution holdout improves monotonically in every arm (A .21 to .40), so it cannot see the drift; the reference/KL run in #9735 shows the same entropy rise (1.0 to 2.2 by step 10) and had only that holdout. Length stops stay under 9% throughout training and are not the cause.

A's agentic behaviour drifts the same way. Its replies on the pivot validation turns grow 1.5 to 2 times by step 12, A8 overflows the 73K-token context in 17% of SWE-bench tasks (every non-zero agent exit in A8 and A12 is a context-window overflow), and in the A12 eval the median model call took 17 s against 3.6 s for the other runs: 171 of 500 trials hit the 30-minute agent budget, 122 of them then timing out in the verifier. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors, and the retries have moved A12 from .244 to .272 so far.

## Decision rules

The first rule, B above A on SWE-bench Verified by more than two paired standard errors with the reasoning benchmarks within noise, holds at steps 4 and 8 (SE about 2 points; B−A +6.0 and +9.2). At step 12 no arm has the reasoning benchmarks within noise. The second rule, B ≈ C, fails at every step by 6 to 12 points, and the logged informative-group counts attribute part of that to C's weaker signal. Confidence is limited by one seed per arm; the B effects are 3 to 5 standard errors on SWE-bench, and isolated p<.05 cells such as B8 vs A8 on AIME24 (−4.0, p=.04) are what a hundred comparisons produce.

## What it took

- Layout: 16 H100 nodes per arm, 10 policy nodes with the colocated reference and 12 inference engines at DP4/EP4 on the other 6; 11 to 16 hours per 12-step run.
- Runtime: MarinSkyRL branch `dml/mixed-rlvr-runtime` at bfef1308, seven commits over the fork's main at 563658e5: verifyit pivot graders for the Nemotron pivot rows, per-agent `pivot_reward`, the SWE pivot agent name, null message fields in Parquet prompts, request tools passed as chat tools, and a retry for vLLM engine gangs that die during startup. marin-community/MarinSkyRL#992 carries the first six. The fork was archived on 2026-10-20, so these need porting into `vendor/skyrl` once the verifyit graders from #10215 are published.
- Evaluation: the October 5 verified paired-eval stack (`held/eval-october17-verified` at f9990d36) plus fixes on branch `dml/eval-october17-verified-pivot-mixed-rlvr`: a localhost relay that reports the Iris proxy's 404 during an inference-server reschedule as 503 for ten minutes so Evalchemy retries; Daytona verifier thread limits, because native test libraries sized their pools to the host and exhausted the 300 s verifier timeout; mini-swe-agent pinned to litellm 1.105.1 after an MCP import regression; a 24 h placement budget that treats Kueue's SchedulingGated state as unplaced; the Run:ai streamer load format for staged HF exports; `--cluster-config` so evaluations submit as the openathena.ai login after the contractor service account's default budget demoted jobs to batch band; and an export barrier that waits for the HF export job and verifies its shards before evaluating.
- Scoring: strict first-trial SWE-bench with the fullest run per arm and step; TBLite majority of 3 trials; repeated-trial benchmarks averaged per question.

## Next

- Final A12 SWE-bench number when the retry wave ends.
- A seed-43 replicate of all three arms launched 2026-10-20 21:29 UTC as the openathena.ai login, A on cw-us-east-02a, B and C on cw-rno2a: [A](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/5thdcjv5), [B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/v8o72kqn), [C](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/pivot-mixed-rlvr/runs/2rjy7l3n). C has been preempted three times by production-band jobs on rno2a and restarts from scratch each time.
- The recipe needs a drift fix before running past 8 steps: a stronger KL coefficient, a lower learning rate, dropping the entropy bonus, or a length penalty. The optional p arms (B-10, B-30) remain open; the second seed was prioritized.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 Final A12 SWE-bench number: .282, 141 of 500 solved. Harbor's retries of the verifier timeouts finished at 07:47 UTC with every trial scored, so the provisional .272 above becomes .282 and the step-12 row of the SWE-bench table reads A .282, B .308, C .244: B vs A +2.6 (p=.21), B vs C +6.4 (p=.002), C vs A −3.8 (p=.048), B vs REF +4.8 (p=.025), A vs REF +2.2 (p=.28). Steps 4 and 8 are unchanged, and the 54 evaluations of the seed-42 series are complete.

A12's first-pass strict score was .244, with 128 trials that ended in a verifier timeout after the agent had used its 30-minute budget. Harbor retries verifier timeouts as infrastructure errors; the retry wave, run at 16 trials at a time instead of the first pass's full concurrency, scored all of them and lifted A12 by 3.8 points. Those timeouts were therefore partly load-induced rather than a property of the policy, although A12's agents still ran about five times slower per model call than the other arms and overflowed the 73K context in 40 tasks. The step-12 reading changes from B ahead of A by 6 points to B ahead by 2.6 points, not significant; B's lead over A at steps 4 and 8 (+6.0, +9.2) and over C at every step is unaffected, and A's own SWE-bench trajectory is flat (A12 vs A4 −0.6, p=.81).

Seed-43 replicate: all three arms finished 12 steps (B at 08:08 UTC, A and C at about 13:55 UTC; C restarted three times after production-band preemptions on cw-rno2a). Exports for A steps 4, 8 and 12, B steps 4, 8 and 12 and C steps 8 and 12 are done or running, with their evaluations queued behind verified exports. C's step-4 checkpoint was pruned by the trainer before its export request landed, so the replicate has no C step-4 point. The two-seed results will follow when those 48 evaluations finish.

Plain SFT recovers less; merging is a cheap partial substitute at half strength only. ## Caveats - One evaluation pass per checkpoint except the stated repeats; plain SFT's 803-vs-603 selection used two passes each. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons or checkpoint selection. - Both primary targets are test-exposed (training-is-test); the held-out MMLU-Pro questions are an additional probe, never a selection input. - The RS-SFT demo selector used an older answer-extraction rule than the evaluator: 14 of its 1,400 MMLU-Pro demos are wrong under the evaluator's rule, 15 prompts would have been gained and 1 lost, 45 would have used a different sample. Reported as trained; no corrected run. - Two records (B and MOPD-100 on MMLU-Pro) had a retried evaluation attempt; all numbers come from each record's pinned FineStore manifest (an earlier reading gave B 43.9 and MOPD 65.3 on the subset). - Evaluation infrastructure cost 1,752.6 H100-h of serve time, 894.5 of it in 31 groups that produced no record (serves left running on stale endpoints, #10030). ## Links | | | |---|---| | Full report with record manifest | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850 | | Single-expert experiment | #9920, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 | | Record manifest (machine-readable) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/records-manifest-20261013.json` | | Canonical MMLU-Pro labels and subset | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/` | | GLM traces and captured prompts | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/glm-bench-traces/` | | Demo pools | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/teacher-traces/mopd2/` | | MOPD config | https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/76fc4be980aff1b14a42bfa549b5fe7479744701/cloud/iris/configs/snowball_mopd2_cruxeval_mmlupro.yaml | | Merge tools | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974 | | GPU-hour method | https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298 | | Trace browser | https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/ | Weights are being uploaded to Hugging Face under open-athena; the S3 paths above will be replaced by HF links as each lands.

🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

## Summary

E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. RS-727 and MOPD-100 are the selected finals of their arms (RS-727 similar to 546, MOPD-100 similar to 50 on every target). They use unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access. Plain-SFT step-803 was selected on two-pass means. The RS arm's demo selector used a different answer-extraction rule from the evaluator (quantified under Caveats). Weight merging at half strength scores above B in both domains with no training (CruxEval input 76.5, output 67.6; MMLU-Pro subset 63.2), below the trained arms on CruxEval output; the full-strength task-arithmetic merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs. Training-gang allocations: RS-SFT 93.6 H100-h, MOPD 557.9 (2 epochs, 7 nodes; plus 28.3 of export-only jobs). Evaluation serve allocation across the 82 eval groups: 1,752.6 H100-h, of which 894.5 in 31 groups with no successful eval child (details under Costs).

## Setup (unchanged from #9920 except where stated)

B = [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab). E = #9920's CruxEval expert (step-272; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)). E_2 ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254 @ acb97183](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254/tree/acb97183af633533df4f4f63d83adc1e0a7a9748) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task157-e2/checkpoints/karan/e2-mmlupro-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.09.1/hf/step-254`)) = B + full SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe (AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer, frozen router bias, 32 H100), 1,359 usable traces over a seeded category-proportional draw of whole question-text groups (1,589 questions = 1,606 docs); the other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and used as an additional probe (prior exposure of either split during B's own training is not ruled out; both primary targets are test-exposed). Labels: the GLM collection had keyed the dataset by question text, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold; every doc was re-joined to TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec76` by exact question + ordered options (artifacts and SHA-256 at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`, independently verified against the pinned source and captured prompts; verification artifact `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/task162-candidate-verification-v4/`). Transfer arms start from B with matched AdamW hyperparameters (LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 1.0) and frozen router bias, implemented in Levanter for SFT and Megatron for MOPD. The shared evaluation universe has 3,206 prompts (1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro). Plain SFT trains four epochs on 3,206 sample-zero demonstrations; RS-SFT trains four epochs on 2,903 covered prompts. MOPD runs two epochs with four rollouts per sampled prompt and domain-routed teachers (100 optimizer updates of 64 prompts; 50 per epoch). These budgets are not token- or compute-matched. MOPD = MarinSkyRL on-policy distillation with two pinned teachers, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (sampled reverse KL, 4 rollouts per prompt, 1:1 route mix). Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). Merges = #9974 tools, B anchor, E and E_2 donors: task arithmetic at a = b = 0.5 and a = b = 1.0, and TIES (density 0.5, a = b = 1.0); CPU only.

## Frozen evaluator

Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (recorded in every record's `eval_runtime`; the `c131e5ab` label in earlier text was an unused code constant and has been corrected in #9920), vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

## Results, MMLU-Pro

(Single pass per checkpoint; subset % / held-out % / all %; Δ = paired vs B on the subset, pp with 95% group bootstrap; B 44.46 / 44.05 / 44.11; E 60.34 / 59.76 / 59.84; E_2 66.44 / 63.97 / 64.30).

## Results, CruxEval and probes

(CruxEval input / output pass@1 of 800 each; GSM8K flexible; single pass unless stated).

| Model | CruxEval in / out | GSM8K | MATH500 | GPQA-D (198×3) | IFEval inst-strict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [B](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab) | 55.4 / 57.75 | 90.4 | 89.8 | 41.9 | 81.1 |

| mixed SFT-RS steps 182 / 364 / 546 | 76.25 / 74.6; 75.1 / 74.6; 78.75 / 76.0 | 92.1; 92.9; 94.8 | | | |

## Paired deltas (pp, 95% bootstrap)

All plain-803-versus-other-model intervals below use its pass 1; both passes are shown in the tables, and selection uses their mean. CruxEval vs B (in / out): MOPD-100 +26.75 [+23.0, +30.5] / +18.6 [+15.0, +22.25]; RS-727 +21.9 [+17.9, +25.75] / +19.5 [+15.75, +23.1]; plain-803 +20.0 [+16.0, +24.0] / +13.75 [+9.9, +17.5]; TA-0.5 +21.1 / +9.9; TIES +17.4 / +10.4. The following CruxEval-versus-E deltas use E's first CruxEval pass (635/800 input, 562/800 output), not the two-pass E mean displayed in the table; plain-803 deltas here use its first pass, and both plain passes are reported together for selection. CruxEval vs E: MOPD-100 +2.75 [−0.5, +5.9] / +6.1 [+2.9, +9.4]; RS-727 −2.1 [−5.6, +1.5] / +7.0 [+3.75, +10.4]; plain-803 −4.0 [−7.75, −0.4] / +1.25 [−2.0, +4.6]; TA-0.5 −2.9 / −2.6; TIES −6.6 / −2.1. MMLU-Pro vs E_2 (subset / held-out): MOPD-100 −2.2 [−4.5, +0.1] / +0.4 [−0.5, +1.3]; RS-727 +1.7 [−0.5, +4.2] / +0.8 [−0.2, +1.8]. Cross-arm (selected finals): RS-727 − MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro +4.0 [+1.6, +6.3] / +0.4 [−0.5, +1.4]; CruxEval −4.9 [−8.1, −1.6] / +0.9 [−2.1, +3.75]. RS-727 − plain-803 MMLU-Pro +5.8 [+3.5, +8.2] / +1.9 [+1.0, +2.9]. Experts across domains: E on MMLU-Pro +15.9 [+13.5, +18.3] over B on the subset without training on it; E_2 on CruxEval −0.9 / −4.9 vs B. IFEval, official instruction-level strict (sum of correct instructions over 834 instructions, prompt-resampling bootstrap): E − B −2.2 [−4.7, +0.2]; E_2 − B −0.8 [−3.2, +1.4]; RS-727 − B −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24] (loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 − B −1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] (loose +0.24 [−2.02, +2.48]); RS-727 − E −0.60 [−3.05, +1.93]; MOPD-100 − E +1.08 [−1.42, +3.57]; RS-727 − MOPD-100 −1.68 [−4.21, +0.95]. GPQA-D (198 questions × 3 repeats, per-question means, question bootstrap): RS-727 − B +15.7 [+10.4, +21.0]; MOPD-100 − B +5.6 [+0.7, +10.4]; RS-727 − MOPD-100 +10.1 [+5.7, +14.5]; RS-727 − E_2 +9.9 [+5.4, +14.5].

**Selection (frozen rule: final checkpoint unless a target metric is lower with the interval excluding 0; then a second pass on the last two and the two-pass means decide; the held-out probe is never an input).** Mixed SFT-RS: step-727 vs 546 similar on MMLU-Pro subset (+1.0 [−1.25, +3.3]) and CruxEval (−1.5 [−5.0, +1.9] / +1.25 [−1.9, +4.4]) → step-727 selected. Mixed SFT: step-803 vs 603 was lower on CruxEval input in pass 1 (−3.9 [−7.5, −0.25]) → second pass on both. On per-item two-pass means (paired, bootstrap over problems / question groups), 803 − 603 = CruxEval input −2.25 [−4.94, +0.38], output −0.12 [−2.56, +2.50], MMLU-Pro subset +1.56 [−0.09, +3.19] (held-out +1.00 [+0.33, +1.63], not a selection input): similar on every target → step-803 selected. The pass-to-pass swings at fixed weights (603 CruxEval input 79.25 → 75.4; 803 MMLU-Pro subset 62.39 → 61.71) are the run-to-run measurements this experiment has; pass-1 intervals do not include them. MOPD: step-50 has two valid CruxEval records, 641/585 from the first group (`20261011-035349`, whose MMLU-Pro and GSM8K evals failed) and 644/608 from the retry group (`20261013-023108`, which produced all three records); no rule fixed before scoring chose between them, and the retry record was used as the selection input because its group is the one that completed. Step-100 vs step-50 (paired, single pass each, retry record): MMLU-Pro subset −0.81 [−2.99, +1.55], CruxEval +1.62 [−1.50, +4.75] / +0.38 [−2.62, +3.38] → similar on every target → step-100 selected; the held-out probe favours step-50 by 1.2 pp [−2.08, −0.36], reported as context. Sensitivity with both step-50 CruxEval passes (step-100 single pass vs the per-problem two-pass mean of step-50, 80.31 / 74.56): +1.81 [−0.94, +4.50] / +1.81 [−1.00, +4.56]; same decision. Merges: single artifacts, no selection.

## Reading the result

(1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

## Caveats

One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). comments.body:
🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages; cosines are given against E and against E₂.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro) | 0.035 | 0.64 | 0.043 | 0.067 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 12.9 | 0.21 vs E | 0.37 | 0.06 | 0.38 |
| Mixed plain SFT step 803 | 0.180 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.42 | 0.033 | 0.53 | 56.3 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.40 / 0.50 |
| Mixed RS-SFT step 727 | 0.171 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.40 | 0.030 | 0.49 | 54.7 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.42 / 0.51 |
| MOPD update 100 | 0.045 | 0.13 | 0.099 | 0.12 | 0.008 | 0.084 | 25.2 | 0.05 / 0.05 | 0.11 / 0.13 | 0.07 / 0.07 | −0.14 / −0.15 |
| Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 0.031 | 0.53 | 0.041 | 0.064 | 0.13 | 0.11 | 12.1 | 0.71 / 0.69 | 0.82 / 0.82 | 0.60 / 0.56 | 0.78 / 0.71 |
| Merge TIES d = 0.5 | 0.043 | 0.73 | 0.057 | 0.084 | 0.19 | 0.14 | 17.2 | 0.73 / 0.69 | 0.75 / 0.73 | 0.73 / 0.65 | 0.84 / 0.69 |

Reading:
- The two experts are built the same way and look the same: 0.035–0.036% of B's norm overall, change concentrated in attention (0.65%), router (0.15–0.17%) and LM head, expert MLPs nearly untouched, 13% of weights changed. Their deltas share a direction (cosine 0.21 overall, 0.37 in attention, 0.38 at the LM head) while their expert-MLP changes are nearly independent (0.06), consistent with a common change in how the model answers (both experts start using their reasoning block on far more prompts) on top of domain-specific MLP changes.
- The mixed SFT arms move the weights most (0.17–0.18% overall, 55–56% of weights changed, expert MLPs 0.38–0.40%), 5× more than the experts whose text they train on, and in a direction almost orthogonal to both experts' deltas (cosine ≈0.02 overall and in the expert MLPs; 0.06 in attention). Only the LM head aligns (0.40–0.51).
- MOPD moves the weights a quarter as much as the SFT arms (0.045% overall, 25% of weights changed), again nearly orthogonal to the experts (0.05–0.13), with the LM head moving against both experts (−0.14 / −0.15). It recovers both experts' scores anyway.
- The merges are, by construction, the experts' deltas: TA 0.5 is their average (cosine 0.69–0.71 with each, magnitude 0.031%), TIES keeps the larger of the two per weight (0.043%, attention 0.73%). They sit far from where the trained arms end up (cosine between merge and arm deltas not computed here).
- Net: four different weight changes, differing in size by 5× and nearly orthogonal in direction, all land within a few points of the experts on both domains. The transfer is not a recovery of the expert's parameters; it is a re-learning of the behaviour from a different starting direction, which is also why the arms' off-domain scores (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D, IFEval) do not simply track the experts'.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights (two values = vs E / vs E₂). Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on the delta-direction question: is the MOPD update "nearly orthogonal" to the expert update, or aligned beyond chance?

## Method

Deltas against the student B (`Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ fdc3c3c5) for expert E (CruxEval, step 272), expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro, step 254), the MOPD update (step 100) and the two mixed SFT arms (plain step 803, RS step 727). Three measures per component: cosine, sign agreement on weights changed in both, and subspace overlap, the share of a delta's energy inside the reference delta's top-k singular directions per matrix (k holding 50% of the reference energy), against two nulls: a random k-dim subspace and the reference delta with entries permuted within each matrix. The run reproduces the cosines posted above exactly. Script: `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_subspace.py` on branch `task/239` (4c99d4d9a4).

## Result

Overlap with E's half-energy subspace, as a multiple of the random null:

| Component | E₂ (peer expert) | MOPD | plain SFT | RS-SFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | 3.4× | 3.5× | 2.4× | 2.4× |
| Expert MLPs | 1.5× | 1.6× | 1.3× | 1.3× |
| Shared experts | 3.9× | 3.4× | 1.7× | 1.8× |
| Router | 2.0× | 2.8× | 1.7× | 1.6× |
| LM head | 295× | 198× | 397× | 407× |

Cosine and sign agreement with E, all weights: E₂ 0.21 / 0.55; MOPD 0.049 / 0.56; plain SFT 0.021 / 0.53; RS-SFT 0.023 / 0.53. In attention MOPD reaches 0.10 / 0.68 against E₂'s 0.38 / 0.71.

## Reading

- Cosine 0.05 over 6.7e10 weights is about 12,000 chance SDs (1/√n = 3.9e-6), so "beyond chance" is a weak bar. The informative controls are the SFT arms (same student, same prompts, same expert texts) and the peer expert.
- Against those controls, MOPD shares direction with the experts more than the SFT arms do, in every component except the LM head, and relative to the random null it sits close to the peer expert in attention and expert MLPs. The permuted null equals the random null everywhere, so the excess comes from the experts' dominant singular directions, not from their entry distribution.
- The shared part is small in energy: 0.24% of MOPD's update lies along E's delta, and 16% inside E's half-energy subspace against 10% for a random subspace. The posted conclusion stands: the transfer is mostly a different weight change that reaches the same behaviour.
- The LM head reverses the pattern: the SFT arms align strongly with the experts there (cos 0.40 to 0.51), while MOPD moves inside the same narrow top directions with the opposite sign (cos −0.14, sign agreement 0.39).
- None of the deltas is rank-1: participation ratios are 20 to 90 directions per matrix. The experts' attention deltas are the most concentrated (top-10 directions hold 80% of their energy); MOPD's is more spread (39%), the SFT arms' more still (24%).

## Limits

Correlational geometry only; no ablation, so no causal claim about the recovered scores. Cross-step self-consistency of the MOPD direction could not be measured because only step 100 exists. The bf16 exports hide changes below half an ulp, so every measure covers only what survived rounding.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
The agent above put some numbers together for "how orthogonal" the task vectors really are for each experiment arm. This is related to @penfever 's [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6201304545) about how the Frobenius norm of the task vector for MOPD is significantly smaller than SFT's.

However, I realized something else that I put in the experiment setup but forgot about: **The MOPD arm's batch size was effectively 16x higher than the SFT arm's with the same LR and fewer steps** . This might explain the whole difference. Specifically, they were "prompt matched", with each epoch seeing 3200 unique prompts / epoch. Specifically:

* SFT had 16 demonstration rows / step
  *  x 200 steps / epoch x 4 epochs = 12800 rollouts
  *  LR 1e-6
* MOPD had 64 prompts x 4 student rollouts / step x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 3200 prompts
  * x 50 steps / epoch x 2 epochs = 25600 rollouts 
  * LR 1e-6

As for why, at the time:
* We had known SFT runs on Snowball that used a 1e-6 LR, and I think even after doing sweeps in #10213 , that seems to be a good LR for this class of experiments
* We had existing M/OPD experiments under the proof-of-life experiments that used the 256 rollouts + 1e-6 LR
* MOPD needed more rollouts / batch to keep it from being as rollout-constrained
* MOPD by construction would see more unique sequences / epoch anyways if they started with the same dataset. 

Either way, we can do an experiment increasing MOPD LR to 4e-6, computed by sqrt(MOPD batch  / SFT batch) ( 1e-6) = 4 * 1e-6.

We'll also run for 4 epochs. This will give us a better sense of whether MOPD was under-stepped. 

Another difference I should note that won't change: MOPD is running using Megatron (our SkyRL setup), SFT is using Levanter

- **MOPD.** Each checkpoint carries its export job (about 14 H100-h). Measured allocation-to-checkpoint for MOPD, as a cross-check: ≈317 / ≈531 H100-h.
- **Trained tokens.** As in #9920: SFT from the row manifests × epochs, MOPD from per-update scored tokens.
- **Excluded.** Evaluations, building the experts, and the evicted plain attempt (14.2 H100-h).

Reading:
- **The arms reach different targets.** RS-SFT reaches E₂'s MMLU-Pro subset level at update 546 (93.7 H100-h); MOPD never does (best 65.0). MOPD reaches E's CruxEval input level at update 50 (292.8 H100-h); neither SFT arm does (best 78.75 / 79.25).
- **Matched GPU-hours.** Both SFT runs ended (117 and 131 H100-h) before MOPD's first checkpoint (292.8). At the SFT arms' final cost, a straight line from B to MOPD update 50 puts MOPD at about 53 MMLU-Pro and 65–67 / 65–66 CruxEval. That is an interpolation, not a measurement.
- **Trained tokens.** MOPD trains on 7–9× more tokens than the SFT arms; most of them (56.7M) come in its first epoch.

Caveats:
- This is not a matched-compute experiment; the arms differ in optimizer, batch geometry and verifier access.
- Single passes unless marked.
- MOPD's W&B history logged 99 of 100 updates.
- The RS demo selector used a different MMLU-Pro answer rule from the evaluator, which affects 1% of its demos.

issues.body:
🤖 Comparison of the Marin 67B-A2B checkpoints from #6044 and #8813 against Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, scored the same way lm-eval scored the open-weight baselines in #8824.

## TL;DR

- On the Paloma test split, the 65k-context checkpoint (step 156k) gets **0.7812** macro BPB and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base gets **0.8397** (−7.0%). Our model is lower on 15 of 16 subsets; M2D2 S2ORC is the exception (+2.4%).
- On the 7 legacy UncheatableEval subsets, it gets **0.5178** vs **0.5245** (−1.3%). We are lower on Wikipedia, BBC News and AO3. Qwen is lower on C++ (by 5.7%), arXiv Physics and arXiv CS; Python is a tie.
- Against Gemma 4 26B-A4B, the pre-trained base (`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B`; the instruction-tuned model is the separate `-it` repo), the 65k checkpoint gets **0.7812** vs **0.8100** on Paloma (−3.6%). Our model is lower on 12 of 16 subsets; Gemma is lower on C4 100 domains, 100 subreddits, Gab and Twitter AAE. On the 7 UncheatableEval subsets Gemma is lower: **0.5138** vs our **0.5178** (ours is 0.8% higher). We are lower on GitHub Python, arXiv Physics and arXiv CS; Gemma is lower on Wikipedia, GitHub C++, BBC News and AO3. All Gemma numbers are our own lm-eval run, not #8824's (see "Gemma: correction to the #8824 numbers").
- **Correction:** an earlier version of this issue used #8824's Gemma Paloma macro of 0.8494 and reported our lead as −8.0%. Run through our lm-eval setup, Gemma gets 0.8100. The difference is concentrated in short-document subsets (Twitter AAE 2.564 vs 2.016, Gab 1.469 vs 1.287), so #8824's Gemma setup differs from ours in a way that isn't context length. Qwen's #8824 numbers do reproduce under our setup.
- At 32k context, Paloma macro is **0.7716** (ours), **0.8278** (Qwen, −6.8%) and **0.7837** (Gemma, −1.5%). Gemma gains more from the longer context (−3.2%) than ours (−1.2%) or Qwen (−1.5%). UncheatableEval does not change, because every document fits in 4k tokens.
- The 262k context extension (qk_mult 1.75, 8× long-document skew, step 157k) is slightly lower again: 0.7795 Paloma, 0.5171 UncheatableEval.
- Marin's in-training Paloma numbers are not directly comparable to the #8824 open-model rows: Levanter scores Paloma **val**, lm-eval scores Paloma **test**, and Levanter packs documents. See "Why earlier Marin numbers differ" below.

![BPB per eval: 65k ckpt, 262k ckpt, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, Gemma 4 26B-A4B base](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/e5caad072b27080a4b034e2c683beb1029032277/experiments/grug/moe/eval_67b_a2b_vs_open_bases_bpb.png)

## Results

All numbers are bits per byte (lower is better). Document counts match Qwen's lm-eval run exactly for every subset.

| Falcon RefinedWeb | 1,711 | 0.7124 | 0.7112 | 0.7788 | 0.7310 | -8.5% | -2.5% |

| M2D2 S2ORC | 167 | 0.6183 | 0.6172 | 0.6037 | 0.6480 | +2.4% | -4.6% |

| UncheatableEval subset | Docs | 65k ckpt | 262k ckpt | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | Gemma 4 26B-A4B | 65k vs Qwen | 65k vs Gemma |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Wikipedia English | 1,000 | 0.5876 | 0.5870 | 0.6176 | 0.5842 | -4.8% | +0.6% |
| GitHub Python | 973 | 0.2483 | 0.2476 | 0.2479 | 0.2558 | +0.2% | -2.9% |
| GitHub C++ | 998 | 0.2605 | 0.2601 | 0.2465 | 0.2429 | +5.7% | +7.3% |
| BBC News | 1,081 | 0.6298 | 0.6288 | 0.6667 | 0.6130 | -5.5% | +2.7% |
| arXiv Physics | 1,000 | 0.5544 | 0.5537 | 0.5461 | 0.5595 | +1.5% | -0.9% |
| arXiv CS | 1,000 | 0.5438 | 0.5436 | 0.5386 | 0.5533 | +1.0% | -1.7% |

| **Macro (7)** | 7,052 | **0.5178** | **0.5171** | **0.5245** | **0.5138** | **-1.3%** | **+0.8%** |

## Method

The scorer reimplements lm-eval 0.4.12 `loglikelihood_rolling` for grug checkpoints. Evalchemy pins upstream lm-eval v0.4.12, and Qwen's run used the stock `local-completions` backend with `max_length=4096`, `tokenizer_backend=huggingface`, `tokenized_requests=True` (from its results JSON).

- **Documents:** scored one at a time, nothing packed. Paloma test split (revision `65cd6fc`, 154,440 docs); UncheatableEval Sept 1–14 2025 dumps (7,052 docs).
- **Windows:** lm-eval's API backend uses `max_length - 1` and rolls with `max_length - 1` again, so windows predict 4,094 tokens, each conditioned on the single preceding token, except the final window of each document, which keeps a full 4,094-token left context. The window code was checked against lm-eval's own `get_rolling_token_windows` + `make_disjoint_window` for lengths 0–30,000.
- **Tokenization:** HF tokenizer with `add_special_tokens=False`. The prefix token is BOS when the tokenizer has one (Marin: `<|begin_of_text|>`; Qwen has no BOS, so lm-eval used `<|endoftext|>`).
- **BPB:** summed NLL ÷ UTF-8 bytes of the document text, per subset; macro is the unweighted mean over subsets (matches Qwen's reported 0.839683).
- **Model:** params-only restore on a v4-64 in us-central2, bf16 compute. Before scoring, each job checks `qk_mult`, width, depth, expert counts, sliding window, `disable_long_rope` and `disable_pko` against the training run's `.executor_info` and fails on any mismatch (65k ckpt: qk_mult 1.57; 262k ckpt: 1.75).
- **Qwen numbers:** taken from the #8824 results file [qwen-results.json](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/hero-open-weight-ppl/2026.09.05.1/qwen-results.json). A rerun of Qwen with lm-eval 0.4.12 reproduced them (Paloma 0.8404 vs 0.8397, UncheatableEval 0.5246 vs 0.5245; [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lz5m5lk3)).
- **Gemma numbers:** our run of `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B` revision `24548b6` with lm-eval 0.4.12 `local-completions` (`max_length=4096`, HF tokenizer, tokenized requests) against vLLM 0.30.0 on 8×H100, on the same 154,440 Paloma and 7,052 UncheatableEval documents: [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/3rzcpy9e) (lm-eval results JSON attached). This is the same setup that reproduced Qwen.

- 4k packed Levanter eval used for the comparison below: [`eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_seq4k.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9cb1640a79a8df9fc21d4abcff916178eee9d057/experiments/grug/moe/eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_seq4k.py)

## Reproduce

```bash
git checkout 9cb1640a79
# one job per checkpoint; each runs Paloma (test) and UncheatableEval as two child jobs on v4-64 us-central2
.venv/bin/iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --region us-central2 -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
    -- python -m experiments.grug.moe.eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling step156k
.venv/bin/iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --region us-central2 -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
    -- python -m experiments.grug.moe.eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling skew8
git checkout e5caad072b && uv run --with matplotlib python experiments/grug/moe/plot_67b_a2b_vs_open_bases_bpb.py bpb.png
```

Each child job takes 5–15 minutes once the slice is up. The 262k job ran exactly this commit. The 65k job ran an earlier revision of the same file with identical scoring code but without the startup config check; its config was checked separately (qk_mult 1.57).

## Context length: 4k vs 32k

All three models rescored with lm-eval `max_length=32768` (ours: same grug scorer, [W&B Paloma](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling32768); Qwen: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/rfqtrvbi); Gemma: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/qtfi2lqk)). The 4k columns are our own runs of each model; Qwen's 4k column is the rerun, not #8824. Only documents longer than 4,094 tokens change, so Gab, 100 subreddits and Twitter AAE are identical at both lengths, as expected. UncheatableEval is unchanged for all three models (its longest document is 4,082 tokens).

| Paloma subset | Ours 4k | Ours 32k | Qwen 4k | Qwen 32k | Gemma 4k | Gemma 32k | Ours vs Qwen (32k) | Ours vs Gemma (32k) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4chan | 0.8254 | 0.8007 | 0.8828 | 0.8425 | 0.8773 | 0.7979 | -5.0% | +0.4% |
| C4 100 domains | 0.6513 | 0.6507 | 0.7047 | 0.7038 | 0.6484 | 0.6469 | -7.6% | +0.6% |
| C4 English | 0.6982 | 0.6976 | 0.7553 | 0.7542 | 0.7079 | 0.7059 | -7.5% | -1.2% |
| Dolma v1.5 | 0.6183 | 0.6108 | 0.6585 | 0.6499 | 0.6338 | 0.6197 | -6.0% | -1.4% |
| 100 programming languages | 0.3022 | 0.2836 | 0.3394 | 0.3129 | 0.3471 | 0.3017 | -9.4% | -6.0% |
| 100 subreddits | 0.8707 | 0.8707 | 0.9144 | 0.9144 | 0.8599 | 0.8599 | -4.8% | +1.3% |
| Falcon RefinedWeb | 0.7124 | 0.7112 | 0.7790 | 0.7773 | 0.7310 | 0.7279 | -8.5% | -2.3% |
| Gab | 1.3095 | 1.3095 | 1.4509 | 1.4509 | 1.2869 | 1.2869 | -9.8% | +1.8% |
| M2D2 S2ORC | 0.6183 | 0.5874 | 0.6037 | 0.5701 | 0.6480 | 0.5861 | +3.0% | +0.2% |
| M2D2 Wikipedia | 0.5824 | 0.5721 | 0.6250 | 0.6118 | 0.6283 | 0.5876 | -6.5% | -2.6% |
| Manosphere | 0.8896 | 0.8806 | 0.9312 | 0.9205 | 0.8927 | 0.8777 | -4.3% | +0.3% |
| mC4 | 0.6461 | 0.6421 | 0.7144 | 0.7069 | 0.6853 | 0.6739 | -9.2% | -4.7% |
| Penn Treebank | 0.6755 | 0.6587 | 0.7138 | 0.6898 | 0.8932 | 0.8109 | -4.5% | -18.8% |

| **Macro (16)** | **0.7812** | **0.7716** | **0.8404** | **0.8278** | **0.8100** | **0.7837** | **-6.8%** | **-1.6%** |

## Gemma: correction to the #8824 numbers

#8824's Gemma file gives Paloma macro 0.8494. Our lm-eval setup, which reproduces #8824's Qwen numbers, gives 0.8100 at 4k. The per-subset differences go both ways, so it is not a context-length effect:

| Paloma subset | #8824 | Ours, 4k | Ours, 32k |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Twitter AAE | 2.5644 | 2.0164 | 2.0164 |
| Gab | 1.4689 | 1.2869 | 1.2869 |
| 100 subreddits | 0.8904 | 0.8599 | 0.8599 |
| 4chan | 0.8415 | 0.8773 | 0.7979 |
| M2D2 S2ORC | 0.6173 | 0.6480 | 0.5861 |
| Penn Treebank | 0.8385 | 0.8932 | 0.8109 |
| **Macro (16)** | **0.8494** | **0.8100** | **0.7837** |

Short-document subsets are much worse in #8824 (Twitter AAE, Gab), while some long-document subsets are better in #8824 than in our 4k run (4chan, M2D2 S2ORC, Penn Treebank), which suggests a longer window there. The #8824 Gemma file is a summary without its lm-eval config, so we can't pin down the difference; BOS handling on short documents is one candidate. This issue now uses our own run for every Gemma number.

## Why earlier Marin numbers differ

Same checkpoint (step 156k), three ways of scoring Paloma:

| Scoring | Paloma split | Macro BPB |
|---|---|---:|
| In-training Levanter eval, 65,536-token packed sequences | val | 0.7896 |
| Levanter eval, 4,096-token packed sequences, full coverage | val | 0.8037 |
| lm-eval-exact (this issue) | test | 0.7812 |

- **Split:** lm-eval prefers a task's test split when it has one, and the Paloma template defines both. Levanter's validation sets use val. They are different documents (e.g. Falcon 1,553 val vs 1,711 test; mC4 1,108 vs 1,202).
- **Packing:** on UncheatableEval, where the documents are identical, the 4k packed eval gives 0.5395 and the exact method gives 0.5178. Packing cuts short documents at sequence boundaries and drops each subset's final partial sequence; lm-eval scores every document whole.
- **Context:** going from 65k to 4k packed sequences raised BPB most on long-document subsets (code +10.0%, M2D2 S2ORC +5.6%, RedPajama +5.1%) and barely moved Gab, Penn Treebank and Twitter AAE.

The Hero numbers and forecast in #8824 come from the packed Levanter eval on val, so they share this mismatch with the open-model rows there.

## Caveats

- `uncheatable_eval_hero`, the task #8824 used for Qwen, is not in evalchemy or the marin repo. Its per-subset document counts match ours exactly, but we could not confirm that it scores the raw `text` field.
- Training-data overlap with Paloma is unknown for both models. Paloma's C4, Dolma, RedPajama and Falcon subsets come from web-crawl sources close to our mix; the lead over Qwen is larger on Paloma (−7.0%) than on UncheatableEval (−1.3%).
- One evaluation per checkpoint. Scoring is deterministic, but the 262k vs 65k gap (−0.0017 Paloma, −0.0007 UncheatableEval) is small enough that we would not read much into it.
- Qwen's training compute is not public; #8824 assumes 36T tokens.

## Next

- Score Trinity Mini Base and Ling-lite-base-1.5 with the same lm-eval setup for more same-size base-model points. GPT-OSS-20B and GLM-4.7 Flash have no base checkpoints.
- Confirm the `uncheatable_eval_hero` task definition with the #8824 author.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
🤖  Snowball v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, revision 6783e974, the base selected in #10283) takes about twice as many steps per task as Snowball v0 on agentic coding evals. Under the time and context limits of the eval policy (#10197) that turns into a large number of timed-out trials. Per trial that finishes, v0.1 is the stronger model.

cc @penfever

## What was measured and how

Both models were run on the same two agentic evals, with the same harness, task sets and limits:

- **SWE-bench Verified, random-100**: 100 fixed tasks, run with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 through Harbor at commit 38742b0f. The agent must run the harness's submit command to hand in its patch. Context limit 32,768 tokens.
- **Terminal-Bench Lite, 100 tasks**: 100 fixed tasks, run with the Terminus-2 agent. Each task has an 1,800 second wall-clock limit. Context limit 32,768 tokens.
- Both models served with vLLM on H100s (non-preemptible serve, fixed eval-policy runner at commit 4d45932e39). Snowball v0 is `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12`. The two models share the tokenizer and chat template byte for byte.
- Step counts, submit commands and context-limit endings were counted from the saved trajectories of every trial. A "step" is one model turn (one tool call or one final message).

Results (one trial per task; a few tasks ran twice after infrastructure retries, hence 99 or 110 trials):

| | v0 | v0.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Terminal-Bench Lite: tasks solved | 20 of 99 | 23 of 99 |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: trials that hit the 1,800 s limit | 8 | 49 |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: solve rate on trials that finished in time | 22% | 40% |
| Terminal-Bench Lite: steps per trial, median | 14 | 26 |
| SWE-bench random-100: tasks solved | 33 of 100 | 26 of 100 |
| SWE-bench: trials in which the agent ran the submit command | 70 of 110 | 37 of 100 |
| SWE-bench: trials that ended at the 32,768-token context limit | not counted in that run | 59 of 100 |

A second measurement comes from a data-generation run in which each model writes the opening turns of a task before a larger teacher model continues it, on 2,100 SWE-bench-style tasks and 2,015 terminal tasks, eight samples per task, with a 30,000-token budget per episode:

- The median length of one model turn is the same for both (v0.1 872 tokens, v0 879 tokens, measured over several thousand terminal-task turns).
- The tail differs: v0.1's 99th-percentile turn sits at the 16,384-token per-turn cap, v0's at about 13,000.
- Episodes started by v0.1 run out of the 30,000-token budget before the teacher reaches the submit step more often (72% of the passing SWE episodes, against 64% for v0).

So the extra length is more steps per task and a longer tail per turn, not a longer typical turn.

## Why it matters

- The policy-level selection of v0.1 (#10283, mean paired win rate 0.684) and these agentic evals disagree on which base is better, and the disagreement is explained by the time and context limits rather than by capability.
- Any training that starts from v0.1 inherits the long episodes unless the training data pulls them back. Any v0-vs-v0.1 comparison on agentic evals should report the timeout count next to the score.

## Open questions

1. Is the extra length something the RL run rewarded (v0.1 is 14 updates of RLOO-N RL on the Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02 merge, #10305), or was it already present in that merge before RL? Running the pre-RL merge on the same two evals would separate the two.
2. Does fine-tuning v0.1 on data with short reasoning per turn reduce its step count? A fine-tune of v0.1 on such data is being trained under #10213 and will be measured on the same two evals; the result will be posted here.
3. Should the eval policy report timed-out trials separately from failed ones, so that this kind of base-level difference is visible at selection time?

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The matched-task results show a length and completion problem under the fixed policy limits: v0.1 timed out on 49/99 TBLite trials versus 8/99 for v0, and 59/100 SWE-bench trials reached the context limit. The two checkpoints have different ancestry as well as different training: v0.1 is Step14 RL from the Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02 merge, while v0 is a Campaign3 DARE-Linear merge. That leaves the source of the extra length unresolved; the current measurements do not identify a harness defect.

**Relevant records**
- [#10305](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10305) — Step14 initializer and RL recipe
- [#10213 update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6277328209) — v0.1 SFT arms and shorter-reasoning data
- [#10213 reference screens](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6281042416) — pinned v0.1 task outcomes
- [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) — current scoring and reportability policy

# Proposed Fix

1. Run the pre-RL Campaign2 DARE-TIES-02 merge at revision `153f5369` on the *same fixed* SWE-bench random-100 and TBLite-100 tasks, Harbor `38742b0f`, runner `4d45932e39`, 32,768-token context, and 1,800-second TBLite limit. Match serving and sampling settings to the saved Step14 run; reuse the existing v0 and v0.1 traces. Publish task IDs, pins, scored denominators, and per-task outcomes so the pre-RL-to-Step14 comparison isolates the RL stage.
2. For all three checkpoints, report all-trial solve rate alongside timeout, context-limit, proper submit/finish, steps per trial, and per-turn token tails. Keep model-induced limit exits in the scored denominator and infrastructure failures separate. If the pre-RL merge already has the long tail, investigate the merge lineage; if it does not, inspect Step14 rollout reward and loss-token contribution versus length before choosing an RL length-control ablation. Repeat only comparisons whose score or length difference is within sampling uncertainty.
3. Use the v0.1 reference screens as the control for the v0.1 SFT arms already underway in #10213. Evaluate the same completion and length measures with the same task IDs; a useful mitigation must reduce limit exits and improve all-trial solves without a decisive retention loss. Report completed-trial solve rate as a diagnostic, never as a replacement score.
4. Add timeout, context-limit, and submit/finish counts as companion diagnostics in the next #10197 policy update, coordinated with #10234. Preserve the current limits and selection rule until that update is specified prospectively.

Done when: the paired pre-RL analysis and the v0.1 SFT comparison are posted with these diagnostics, and the policy reporting change is tracked in #10234.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Mechanism per harness, from the same reference runs:

- **Terminal-Bench Lite (Terminus-2)** never ends a trial at the context limit: when the transcript fills, the agent summarizes and continues. The limiter is the 1,800 s wall clock. v0.1: 49 of 99 trials timed out (v0: 8); among trials that finished in time it solved 20 of 50 (v0: 20 of 91). The typical step is barely longer (median completion 1,076 vs 952 tokens); the difference is the tail (66 steps of 16k+ completion tokens vs 6, at about 9 s per 1k tokens on the same server) and twice the steps per task (median 26 vs 14). Context pressure appears as 2.3x the summarization output (1.88M vs 0.83M tokens over the run).
- **SWE-bench (mini-swe-agent 2.1.0)** stops a trial at the 32,768-token context limit. v0.1: 59 of 100 trials ended there, 37 issued the submit command (v0: 70 of 110); median 42 steps per trial.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Frequent timeouts make the agentic scores hard to read. A Terminal-Bench Lite score mixes what the model can solve with how fast it is served: a trial that runs out of wall-clock time counts as a failure even if the model was on track.

| Terminal-Bench Lite, 100 tasks | v0 | v0.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Solved / scored | 20 / 99 | 23 / 99 |
| Trials stopped by the 1,800 s limit | 8 | 49 |
| Solved among trials that finished in time | 20 / 91 (22%) | 20 / 50 (40%) |

v0.1 solves almost twice as many of the trials it finishes, but its headline score is only 3 points higher. Proposals for the eval policy (#10197):
1. Report timed-out trials separately from failures (solved / failed / timed out), so a score drop from time can be told apart from a drop in capability.
2. Add a model-side token budget per trial (total generated tokens) next to the wall-clock limit. Wall-clock time depends on the serving stack and hardware, so the same model can score differently on different setups. A token budget gives the same limit everywhere; the wall-clock limit stays as a safety cap.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Do the TBLite time and context limits explain Snowball v0.1's TBLite score?** These reruns show no clear effect.

We reran v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14` @ 6783e974) on the same 100 TBLite tasks with the same pins. Each rerun changes one setting: the per-trial agent timeout (1,800 → 5,400 s) or the agent's input context (32k → 64k tokens).

| Setting | Solved | Timeouts | Records |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,800 s (reference) | 23 / 100 | 49 | `20261019-213306-v01-reference-smartie-step14-openthoughts-tblite-100-8b8f` |
| 5,400 s | 24 / 100 | 27 | `20261020-164700-v01-tblite-5400-openthoughts-tblite-100-5400-a863` (96 tasks) + `20261021-002828-v01-tblite-5400-openthoughts-tblite-5400-retry4-8803` (4 tasks lost to infra) |
| 1,800 s, 64k input context (reference: 32k) | 26 / 100 (3 unscored) | 30 | `20261021-002906-v01-tblite-64k-openthoughts-tblite-100-64k-358c` |

Per task, 1,800 s vs 5,400 s:

| | Tasks |
|---|---|
| Solved in both | 14 |
| Solved only at 5,400 s | 10 |
| Solved only at 1,800 s | 9 |
| Solved in neither | 66 |
| Unscored in one run | 1 |

- The one-point gain is smaller than the run-to-run churn (10 tasks gained, 9 lost).
- Only 3 of the 10 new solves used more than 1,800 s: server-log-analysis (3,897 s), raft-log-repair-concurrent-access (5,225 s) and rsa-jwt-token-api-redis-blacklist (5,410 s). The other 7 finished in 69–1,211 s, inside the old limit. They did not require the extra wall-time allowance; independent reruns cannot isolate its causal effect.
- Of the 49 trials that timed out at 1,800 s: 7 were solved at 5,400 s, 19 finished but failed, and 23 timed out again.
- Caveat: each 5,400 s trial is a fresh, independent sample, not a continuation of the 1,800 s trial. So this compares two runs, not one run given more time.

Per task, 1,800 s at 32k vs 1,800 s at 64k context: 11 solved in both, 15 only at 64k, 12 only at 32k, 58 in neither, 4 unscored in one run.

- Doubling the input context gives +3 solves, again inside the run-to-run churn (15 gained, 12 lost).
- Of the 49 reference timeouts: 7 solved at 64k, 18 finished but failed, 22 timed out again, 2 unscored.
- Caveat: the 64k trials also ran about 20% faster per completion token (median 11.3 vs 14.3 s of agent wall time per 1k tokens, which includes tool time). Some of the drop in timeouts may come from speed, not context.

Bottom line: neither a 3x timeout nor a 2x context window gives a gain larger than the run-to-run churn. With one run per setting, this does not establish that the settings are equivalent either.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Conclusion of the TBLite time-limit check: the 1,800 s limit was not artificially lowering Snowball v0.1's score.** Tripling the limit changed the score by one task, within sampling noise.

| TBLite-100, Snowball v0.1 (32k context unless noted) | Solved | Timed out |
|---|---|---|
| 1,800 s limit (policy) | 23 / 100 | 49 |
| 5,400 s limit | 24 / 100 | 27 |
| 1,800 s limit, 64k context | 26 / 100 | 30 |

- With 3x the time, 22 fewer trials timed out but only one more task was solved; of the 10 tasks solved only under the long limit, just 3 needed more than 1,800 s, and 9 other tasks flipped the other way. The per-task churn (14 solved under both limits) is what two samples of a noisy model give.
- The longer context moved things the same way: 15 tasks gained, 12 lost, net +3, inside the same noise.
- So the timeouts are a symptom of the model's long trajectories, not the cause of the low score: the trials that run out of time would mostly not have passed with more time.

Details, record ids and the per-task overlap are in the comment above (2026-10-21 02:42 UTC).

issues.author: znichols
issues.body:
Active members of the Open-Athena GitHub organization cannot sign in to `loom.oa.dev`. GitHub returns its 404 page during OAuth authorization, before the callback reaches Loom.

Reproduce:
1. Sign into GitHub with an active Open-Athena member account that is not a `marin-community` organization member.
2. Open `https://loom.oa.dev/api/auth/github/login`.
3. Observe Loom redirect to GitHub OAuth with client ID `Iv23lia1NL3t2ZT0ddoD` and callback `https://loom.oa.dev/api/auth/github/callback`.
4. Observe GitHub return 404 instead of showing the authorization flow.

Expected: any account admitted by Loom's configured `Open-Athena:188075292` organization policy can complete GitHub OAuth. Loom then verifies active organization membership and opens a session.

Confirmed configuration:
- Client ID `Iv23lia1NL3t2ZT0ddoD` belongs to the `loom-oa-dev` GitHub App owned by `marin-community`.
- The App has one installation.
- Its reported permissions omit organization `members: read`. `infra/loom/README.md` requires **Members: Read-only** for membership authorization.
- All four existing `LOOM_DOTENV` secret versions use the same client ID.
- `https://loom.oa.dev/` and `/api/ready` return 200; `/api/auth/github/login` returns the expected 303. The failure is at GitHub authorization, before Loom checks membership.

Fix requires a `marin-community` GitHub App administrator:
1. Verify the App's visibility and user-authorization policy allow intended Open-Athena members to authorize it even when they are not `marin-community` members.
2. Grant organization **Members: Read-only** and approve the resulting installation permission change.
3. If the OAuth credentials change, add a new `LOOM_DOTENV` secret version, update `marin-loom:dotenvSecretVersion` in `infra/loom/Pulumi.marin-loom.yaml`, and deploy the Loom stack.

Done when:
- A test account that is an active Open-Athena member and is not a `marin-community` member can sign in through GitHub.
- `loom.oa.dev` creates an organization-authorized user for that account.
- The account can mint a personal Loom API token and use it against an authenticated read endpoint.
